strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: extending Bayesian self-consistency losses [34] to unlabeled out-of-simulation data enables a genuinely semi-supervised formulation of amortized Bayesian inference that does not require ground-truth parameters, post hoc corrections, or loss of amortization.

The theoretical contribution (Propositions 1–4) cleanly establishes strict properness of the self-consistency losses and shows no trade-off between the simulation-based and self-consistency loss components, including under model misspecification.
The paper is clearly written and well positioned relative to prior robustness work (e.g., Wehenkel et al., Ward et al., Gloeckler et al.), with a candid related-work discussion.

The controlled case study with an analytic reference posterior allows precise quantification (mean/SD bias, MMD), and the ablation grid (dimensionality, number of unlabeled observations, μ*, summary network, estimated likelihood) is sensibly designed.
The reported effect is striking: near-perfect posterior recovery for observation data many standard deviations outside both training spaces, even with as few as 1–4 unlabeled observations.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single, highly contrived toy model (the normal means problem) with a purely synthetic 'misspecification' (a mean shift with σ²_obs = 0.01). Despite repeated claims of applicability to real-world data, no real-world data is used anywhere — even the 'unlabeled' data is simulated. The central empirical claim of robustness to genuine model misspecification is therefore not actually tested.

The claim of a 'major breakthrough in neural ABI' (stated twice, including in bold) is dramatically overclaimed relative to the evidence: one toy model, known-likelihood conditions performing best, and acknowledged failure to match accuracy when the likelihood is estimated.

No comparison to any competing robustness method (e.g., Ward et al. [37], Wehenkel et al. [38], Gao et al. [12], Huang et al. [21]) on the same benchmark; the paper only contrasts against vanilla NPE, making it impossible to judge relative merit.

The setting arguably favors the method: with the simulator's likelihood being well specified for the shifted-observation process, the self-consistency loss drives posteriors toward near-degenerate solutions; it remains unclear what the method does when the likelihood itself is wrong, which is the practically relevant misspecification scenario.

Several important design choices are unexplored: the weight λ, the choice of proposal p_C(θ) (acknowledged to 'influence training dynamics considerably'), sensitivity to unlabeled data coverage relative to test data, and the risk that unlabeled data drawn from a narrow region biases amortization elsewhere.

The theoretical results are largely straightforward consequences of the definition of strict properness applied to a ratio argument; the main novelty over Schmitt et al. [34] is the application context rather than new theory.

The paper self-identifies as 'work in progress' with promised future experiments (benchmarks, challenging geometries, high-dimensional scenarios); as submitted, it does not meet the evidentiary standard of a top-tier venue.
No code release or reproducibility statement is provided, and no variance over training seeds / repeated runs is reported for the headline results.

strengths: The semi-supervised formulation is clearly motivated: training the self-consistency loss on unlabeled, potentially real-world out-of-simulation data is a sensible and somewhat novel combination of existing ideas (self-consistency losses from refs [22, 34] applied to misspecification robustness).

The propositions on strict properness are correct and neatly connect the semi-supervised objective to scoring-rule theory, including a useful caveat about the case where both likelihood and posterior are estimated.

The experimental design, though limited, is controlled and uses an analytic ground-truth posterior with sensible metrics (posterior mean/SD bias, MMD), and ablations over dimensionality, unlabeled data size, and unlabeled data mean are informative.
The related work section positions the method fairly against calibration-set, post-hoc correction, and generalized-Bayes approaches.
weaknesses: Extremely narrow empirical evaluation: all results are on a single toy model (the normal means problem) with a closed-form posterior. No standard SBI benchmarks (SIR, LV, Lotka-Volterra-style simulators, posteriorDB, etc.), no real-world data despite the central claim that the method works on unlabeled data 'originating from any source, including real-world data.' The paper explicitly acknowledges it is work in progress.

Overclaimed significance: statements such as 'a major breakthrough in neural ABI' and 'no existing ABI approach achieves similar degrees of robustness' are unsupported by a single-Gaussian case study. This repeated strong language is not commensurate with the evidence.

The theoretical contribution is thin: the strict-properness results are near-trivial consequences of the definition of a score and largely restate/extend the known results of refs [22, 34]; no analysis of the misspecified regime is given. In fact, properness of the semi-supervised loss under misspecification (Proposition 3) says nothing about which target q converges to when p*(x) != p(x), which is precisely the regime the paper is about—the theoretical motivation for robustness gains under misspecification is essentially absent.

Important practical concerns are unexamined: sensitivity to the weighting lambda, choice of proposal p_C(theta), interaction between the loss and the number/geometry of unlabeled points, behavior when unlabeled data is severely atypical or multimodal, and failure modes (e.g., what happens when the self-consistency loss on out-of-simulation data pulls the estimator toward a degenerate solution).
The estimated-likelihood experiment (Figure 3) shows nontrivial residual bias in posterior SD and MMD, and the paper gives no remedy, further weakening the generality of the claimed robustness gains.

The abstract's assertion that estimation biases 'cannot be fixed in acceptable time by just simulating more training data' is asserted rather than demonstrated—no scaling experiment varying N is shown.

No comparison against any competing robustness method (e.g., Wehenkel et al. [38], Ward et al. [37], Gao et al. [12]) even in the toy setting, so the claimed superiority over prior art is not empirically substantiated.
Reproducibility details are incomplete (no seed/replicate counts, uncertainty quantification in figures appears minimal, no code release mentioned).

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) under model misspecification / out-of-simulation data.

The idea of using unlabeled real-world data via Bayesian self-consistency losses is elegant and, to the authors' credit, clearly positioned relative to prior robustness methods (post-hoc corrections, calibration sets, adversarial regularization), with honest articulation of what the method does not require.
The propositions on strict properness are correct as far as I can verify, and the paper is transparent that strict properness fails when both likelihood and posterior are estimated.
The empirical effect in Figure 1 is striking: near-exact recovery of the analytic posterior far outside the training distribution, where standard NPE collapses, with only 32 unlabeled observations.

The experimental design is sensible for a controlled case study: closed-form ground truth, systematic univariate variation of dimensionality, unlabeled dataset size, unlabeled data location, summary network, and likelihood estimation.
weaknesses: Very limited novelty: the self-consistency loss itself is taken directly from the authors' prior work ([22, 34]). The contribution is essentially applying an existing loss to unlabeled (possibly out-of-simulation) data plus a set of elementary properness proofs. Propositions 1–4 are nearly trivial (a variance-based score is minimized iff its argument is constant; the sum of proper losses is proper).

Evaluation rests on a single, maximally simple model class (the Gaussian normal means problem with a conjugate analytic posterior). No real-world data experiments at all, despite the central selling point being training on unlabeled real data. The footnote explicitly states the paper is work in progress with additional experiments 'to come' — this alone makes it not competitive for acceptance at a top venue.

No comparison against any competing robustness baselines (e.g., Wehenkel et al. [38], Ward et al. [37], robust SBI methods [21, 23, 30], or simply training NPE on augmented/perturbed simulations). The claims of superiority ('no existing ABI approach achieves similar degrees of robustness') are unsupported without such comparisons.

The method critically requires an evaluable likelihood p(x|θ). Under the very misspecification motivating the work, this likelihood is wrong, so the self-consistency loss pulls q toward the (misspecified) model posterior on real data, not toward any ground-truth posterior. The paper does not analyze what the method guarantees under misspecification — the strict properness results target the model posterior and say nothing about accuracy w.r.t. the data-generating process. The encouraging result with an estimated likelihood (Figure 3) comes with admitted residual bias and, as the authors concede, degenerate solutions exist in the joint setting.

The extrapolation result is surprising and under-explained: the consistency loss is evaluated at only M=32 unlabeled points near μ*=3, yet inference remains accurate at μ_obs=11. Why does training the loss at a narrow band of locations yield correct posteriors much farther out? No analysis, ablation of the weight λ, sensitivity analysis, or investigation of failure modes (e.g., what happens when the likelihood is misspecified in a subtler way than a mean shift) is provided.

Overclaiming throughout: 'remarkable improvements', 'major breakthrough in neural ABI' in abstract and discussion. Such language is not warranted by a proof-of-concept on one toy problem without baselines or real data.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: no code release mentioned, no random seeds/repeats or error quantification over training runs (the error bars in Figures 2–3 appear to be over test observations only), and no training-time overhead measurement of the self-consistency loss despite it requiring L=32 additional posterior density evaluations per unlabeled point per iteration.

The claim of 'no trade-off' (Proposition 3) is technically true asymptotically but potentially misleading in the finite-sample regime, where the consistency term on out-of-simulation data could distort pre-asymptotic training dynamics; this is not investigated.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) under model misspecification and out-of-simulation data, a recognized obstacle to the practical adoption of NPE methods.

The core idea is elegant and practically attractive: exploiting Bayesian self-consistency as an unsupervised loss on unlabeled (potentially real) data requires no ground-truth parameters, no post hoc correction, and preserves full amortization speed.

The theoretical contribution is clean: Propositions 1–4 establish strict properness of the self-consistency losses and the combined semi-supervised objective, including the valuable observation that the loss is proper even under misspecification (p*(x) ≠ p(x)) and the honest caveat that properness fails when both posterior and likelihood are estimated jointly.

The experiments show striking effects: near-perfect posteriors on data far outside the training support (normal means problem), robustness with as few as one to four unlabeled observations, persistence up to 100 dimensions, and good agreement with Stan on a real air-traffic case study with clear quantitative improvements (Tables 1–3).

The paper is clearly written, with sensible ablations (dimensionality, unlabeled data size and location, summary networks, estimated vs. known likelihood) and adequate implementation detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the self-consistency loss is taken essentially verbatim from Schmitt et al. [38] and Ivanova et al. [26]; the contribution is the observation that it can be applied to unlabeled/real data, which is a fairly incremental extension of prior work rather than a fundamentally new method or theory.

Overreaching claims: the abstract and discussion claim a 'major breakthrough in neural ABI' and that 'no existing ABI approach achieves similar degrees of robustness,' but this is not substantiated by head-to-head comparisons with existing robustness methods (e.g., post hoc MCMC correction of Ward et al. [41], RKL-based correction of Siahkoohi et al. [39], calibration of Wehenkel et al. [42], robust statistics of Huang et al. [25]). Without these baselines the central comparative claims are unsupported.

Evaluation is narrow: only two case studies (a Gaussian toy model and one 15-country regression with a single real dataset). No standard SBI benchmark suite (e.g., SBI benchmark tasks, posteriorDB tasks) is used, so generalization to other model classes, simulators, and misspecification types remains unverified — precisely the generalization the authors themselves flag as an open question.

Potential circularity in the real-data experiment: metrics are computed relative to Stan on the same 15 countries whose data are used in the self-consistency loss (M = 15 uses all evaluation data in training). The apparent near-perfect agreement in Table 3 may partly reflect fitting the evaluation data rather than genuine amortized robustness; held-out evaluation is not performed or discussed.

The theory, while correct, is near-trivial: the proofs (Appendix A.1) follow immediately from the definition of the variance loss and Bayes' rule, and Proposition 3 follows from additivity of proper losses. The practically relevant case (both posterior and likelihood unknown) is explicitly not covered by the theory, which weakens the theoretical contribution's practical significance.

Several practical concerns are underexplored: sensitivity to the proposal distribution p_C(θ) (acknowledged as influential in [38] but not ablated here), the choice of λ, the risk of the SC loss degrading performance on in-distribution data, training stability/cost overhead relative to standard NPE, and behavior when unlabeled data are themselves contaminated or highly heterogeneous.
Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of any mentioned code release, and there is no variance/uncertainty reporting across training runs (seed sensitivity) for the neural training results.
Some framing issues: the meta-learning framing in Section 1 is asserted but not developed or tested; the connection to semi-supervised learning literature could be deepened.

strengths: The idea of leveraging Bayesian self-consistency on unlabeled out-of-simulation data is sensible and well-motivated, addressing a genuine and important problem in neural amortized Bayesian inference (robustness under model misspecification/simulation gap).

The theoretical framing is clean: the authors clearly identify when the self-consistency loss is strictly proper (Propositions 1-3) and, importantly, honestly discuss when it is not (both posterior and likelihood unknown), which is a common real-world scenario.

The semi-supervised formulation requires no ground-truth parameters for real data, no post-hoc corrections, and preserves amortization, which is a practical advantage over several existing robustness approaches.

The real-data case study (air passenger traffic vs. Stan reference) demonstrates the method beyond purely synthetic settings, and the appendix provides reasonably detailed setup information and additional results.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core self-consistency loss is taken directly from prior work (Schmitt et al. [38], Ivanova et al. [26]); the contribution is essentially a re-application of an existing loss to unlabeled data. The theoretical propositions (e.g., Prop. 3: 'sum of strictly proper losses is strictly proper') are near-trivial, and Prop. 1-2 closely mirror results in [38].

Evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims: only two case studies (a Gaussian normal-means toy model and one real-data autoregressive regression with 15 countries). No standard SBI benchmarks (e.g., SBI benchmark tasks), no comparison against any competing robustness method (Wehenkel et al. [42], Ward et al. [41], Gloeckler et al. [19], generalized Bayesian approaches [16, 34]), despite positioning the work against them.

Overclaiming: statements such as 'a major breakthrough in neural ABI' and 'no existing ABI approach achieves similar degrees of robustness' are not supported by the evidence, which consists of 'initial experiments' on a toy model where the analytic posterior is known and the likelihood is available or easily learned. These claims should be heavily toned down.

Practical applicability is unclear in the likelihood-free regime: the self-consistency loss requires evaluating p(x*|θ). In the toy study this is known; with an estimated likelihood the gains visibly degrade (Figure 4, increased SD bias). The most common SBI setting (intractable likelihood, no close surrogate) is not convincingly addressed, and the discussion defers this to future work.

Potential circularity concerns are not analyzed: when p_C is chosen as the current posterior approximation, the self-consistency loss may reinforce the estimator's own errors rather than correct them; no analysis, diagnostics, or guidance on choice of p_C, L, or λ is provided.

Statistical rigor: number of repetitions/seeds is not clearly reported for the real-data study; metrics are averaged over 15 countries from a single fit, so variability of the proposed method itself (training stochasticity) is unquantified. The M=15 condition effectively uses all data, raising questions about whether the method's benefit is mainly from seeing all data rather than from self-consistency per se.

Reproducibility: no mention of released code or a repository, which is important given the method involves several non-obvious implementation choices (p_C selection, number of SC samples, weighting λ).
Presentation issues: typos ('In pratice', 'reversed signed'), and Figures 5-7 in the appendix are largely redundant.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: using Bayesian self-consistency losses on unlabeled (potentially real) data is a natural but previously unexplored route to robust semi-supervised amortized Bayesian inference, and the positioning relative to prior robustness methods is well articulated.

The theoretical section is correct and useful: Propositions 1–4 establish strict properness of the self-consistency and semi-supervised losses, and the paper is honest about the key limitation that strict properness fails when both likelihood and posterior are unknown (degenerate solutions exist).

The synthetic normal-means study is carefully designed, varying parameter dimensionality, amount of unlabeled data, distribution of unlabeled data, summary networks, and estimated likelihoods, with an analytic ground-truth posterior enabling precise evaluation (bias, SD bias, MMD).

The real-world air traffic case study with a Stan reference shows substantial and practically meaningful improvements (e.g., Wasserstein distances reduced by roughly half or more), demonstrating the idea transfers beyond toy problems.
Practical significance is high if the approach holds up: amortized inference speed is retained, no post hoc correction is needed, and as few as 1–4 unlabeled observations already yield large gains.
weaknesses: Evaluation lacks any comparison against existing robustness or misspecification-mitigation baselines (e.g., Ward et al. [41], Wehenkel et al. [42], Gloeckler et al. [19], Huang et al. [25], Gao et al. [16]). The claim that 'no existing ABI approach achieves similar degrees of robustness' is asserted but never tested empirically, which is a significant gap for a top-tier venue.

The empirical scope is narrow: one synthetic Gaussian model and one small autoregressive regression with only 15 countries and ~15 time points each, single runs without seed variance, confidence intervals, or statistical uncertainty on the air traffic metrics. Generalization claims ('major breakthrough in neural ABI') are much stronger than this evidence supports.

The most practically relevant regime — unknown likelihood — is exactly where the theory breaks down (loss is no longer strictly proper; trivial solutions such as q(θ|x)=p(θ), q(x|θ)∝1 exist), and the experiments show clearly larger residual bias and MMD in this case. The paper acknowledges this but does not analyze when or why the joint training avoids degenerate solutions, nor the role of the proposal p_C(θ) in training dynamics despite noting its influence.

The claimed robustness to data 'far away from both labeled and unlabeled training data' is only demonstrated for shift in the observation mean; robustness to other misspecification types (variance mismatch, structural misspecification, covariate shift in the real study) is not explored, so the generality of the mechanism is unclear.

Strict properness of the semi-supervised loss (Proposition 3) holds for any p*(x) in an asymptotic/idealized sense, but this says little about finite-sample behavior, optimization dynamics, or whether the SC term could distort posteriors on well-specified in-distribution data; no experiment isolates potential accuracy-robustness trade-offs on in-distribution tasks.

Several presentation issues: hyperparameter λ is central to the method but its selection and sensitivity are never discussed; the abstract's 'initial experiments' phrasing and repeated 'major breakthrough' language overclaim; some experiments referenced as complete results are relegated to appendix tables with only aggregate averages.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) under simulation gaps / model misspecification, which is a known blocker for widespread use of ABI in the sciences.

The semi-supervised formulation is elegant and practically valuable: it requires only unlabeled observations (no ground-truth parameters), maintains full amortization at inference time, and can be added to any standard simulation-based objective.

The paper provides theoretical grounding: Propositions 1-4 establish strict properness of the self-consistency and combined semi-supervised losses, and the no-trade-off argument (both components share the same global optimum) is a useful result, even if the proofs are straightforward.

Empirical evaluation covers a nice range of settings: a controllable toy problem with analytic posteriors (enabling MMD and bias quantification with 10 refits and error bars), a real-data application benchmarked against Stan (MCMC), a high-dimensional time-series model (Hodgkin-Huxley), and an image-denoising NPLE setting with 784-dimensional parameters.

The ablations on the toy problem are informative (parameter dimensionality up to 100, number of unlabeled observations down to M=1, distance of unlabeled data from training data, presence of a summary network, estimated vs. known likelihood), and the paper is honest about degradation in the estimated-likelihood case.
Computationally lightweight; the method keeps inference fully amortized, unlike post hoc correction approaches.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to Schmitt et al. [39], who already introduced the self-consistency loss; the main contribution is re-purposing it on unlabeled (out-of-simulation) data plus fairly simple properness proofs. The 'first instantiation of semi-supervised ABI' claim is somewhat overstated given the close relationship to [39].

Missing comparisons to the most relevant competing methods: Wehenkel et al. [44] (data-driven calibration), Ward et al. [43] / Siahkoohi et al. [40] (post hoc correction), Gloeckler et al. [20], and the unsupervised domain adaptation study of Elsemüller et al. [10], which is directly on-topic. Only the naive NPE baseline is evaluated empirically.

The no-trade-off guarantee (Proposition 3) is asymptotic and relies on strict properness of both components; the practical sensitivity to the weighting coefficient λ, to the proposal distribution pC(θ), and to the number of consistency samples L is not systematically ablated, even though the authors themselves note these choices 'influence training dynamics considerably'.

Several robustness claims rest on qualitative evidence: the real-data case studies (air traffic, MNIST) evaluate agreement with a reference rather than rigorous out-of-distribution metrics; the MNIST study is restricted to a single digit ('0') and a single, rather benign misspecification type (extra blur), limiting generality.

In the Hodgkin-Huxley case study, the 'unlabeled' data are actually simulated (from a wider prior), not real data, so this experiment does not test the central semi-supervised claim (using real unlabeled data) but rather improved prior coverage; this distinction is underemphasized.

The method requires a closed-form/differentiable density for the posterior (and a known or learned likelihood), which excludes increasingly popular free-form estimators (flow matching, diffusion); this limitation is acknowledged but restricts applicability.
No explicit statement about code release, which limits reproducibility despite detailed architectural descriptions in the appendix.

Minor issues: the claimed robustness 'far beyond both training spaces' is demonstrated primarily on synthetic shifts with known structure (e.g., Gaussian mean shifts); behavior under more realistic, structured real-world misspecification remains unclear.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important problem: the brittleness of amortized Bayesian inference under simulation gaps and model misspecification, with a clean and practical remedy (semi-supervised training with a Bayesian self-consistency loss on unlabeled data).

Provides formal guarantees: strict properness of the self-consistency and combined semi-supervised losses is proven (Propositions 1–4), and the paper is honest that properness fails in the fully approximate (NPLE) setting.

A diverse set of case studies spanning a controllable toy problem, a real-world autoregressive econometric model with Stan as gold standard, the Hodgkin–Huxley neuroscience model, and high-dimensional image data (MNIST), with sensible ablations over dimensionality, number/mean of unlabeled observations, summary networks, and estimated likelihoods.

Empirically impressive robustness gains, e.g., accurate posteriors with as few as four unlabeled observations versus 1024 labeled ones, and inference remaining reliable far beyond the training distribution.
Maintains amortization and inference speed, and the loss can be added to standard simulation-based objectives without apparent trade-offs.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core self-consistency loss is taken directly from Schmitt et al. [39]; the contribution is primarily its application to unlabeled/out-of-simulation data plus straightforward corollaries of that prior work (the proofs are simple and expected).

Missing comparisons against existing robustness methods: the paper cites close competitors (Ward et al. [43], Siahkoohi et al. [40], Wehenkel et al. [44], Gloeckler et al. [20], generalized Bayesian approaches [17, 35]) but only empirically compares against a vanilla NPE baseline. Claims that the approach 'avoids trade-offs' or is uniquely positioned are therefore not substantiated relative to alternatives.

Theoretical guarantees do not cover the practically relevant regime: strict properness requires either a known likelihood or known posterior; in realistic settings where both are approximated, robustness is only observed empirically, and posterior SD bias persists in the estimated-likelihood case (Figure 7).

Potential circularity and scale concerns in the real-data evaluation: in the air traffic case study, training on M = 15 countries means the self-consistency loss sees the very data used for evaluation; even with M = 4 or 8 the amount of real data is tiny and only one genuine real-world dataset is studied. The MNIST study is restricted to a single digit.

No sensitivity analysis over key hyperparameters (the weighting λ, the proposal p_C for the variance, number of variance samples L), which the authors themselves note can 'influence training dynamics considerably'; also no quantified computational overhead of the extra density evaluations per iteration.
No code or reproducibility statement is provided, which is significant for a methods paper whose utility depends on practical implementation details.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'drastically improves' and 'one of the first instantiations of semi-supervised ABI' rest on a handful of small-scale case studies without statistical comparison to alternative semi-supervised or calibration-based baselines.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under simulation gaps is an important, actively studied challenge, and the semi-supervised angle (using unlabeled real data without ground-truth parameters) is a sensible and practically valuable direction.

The theoretical contribution is sound: the strict properness results (Propositions 1-4) are correct and the proofs are clean, and the observation that the semi-supervised loss has 'no trade-off' since both components share the same minimizer is a nice, reassuring property.

Strong empirical gains demonstrated across diverse settings: the toy multivariate normal study is well-designed with careful factor-by-factor ablations (dimensionality, unlabeled data size, distribution shift), and results on real air traffic data (validated against Stan), Hodgkin-Huxley, and MNIST denoising show the method works on realistic problems with real data.

Notable practical result: robustness improvements with as few as 4-8 unlabeled observations, and accuracy preserved even for observations far outside both labeled and unlabeled training distributions.

Comprehensive appendix with detailed setups, architectures, full result tables, and computational resource reporting supports reproducibility; honest discussion of limitations (e.g., incompatibility with flow matching/score-based estimators).
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the core self-consistency loss is taken from Schmitt et al. [39] (ICML 2024), and the main new element is applying it to unlabeled data plus a largely straightforward extension of properness (Proposition 3 is an immediate consequence of sums of proper losses). The conceptual delta over [39] is modest.

A gap between theory and claims: the strict properness guarantees are with respect to the posterior of the assumed simulator model p(θ|x), not the true data-generating posterior under misspecification. Hence the theory does not actually explain or guarantee the observed robustness under simulation gaps; the robustness claims rest entirely on empirical evidence.

The strongest theoretical guarantee requires a known likelihood, but the MNIST NPLE case study has neither analytic prior nor likelihood, where properness is explicitly shown NOT to hold (Section 2.3). No theory covers the setting where the method's practical benefits are showcased in high dimensions.

Missing sensitivity analyses for key methodological choices: the weight λ of the self-consistency loss and the proposal distribution p_C(θ) are acknowledged to substantially influence training dynamics ('empirical consequences being difficult to anticipate'), yet no ablation or practical guidance is provided.

No comparison against alternative robustness approaches (e.g., Wehenkel et al. [44], post hoc corrections [40, 43], robust/regularized SBI [20, 25]), only NPE vs. NPE+SC. This makes it hard to judge relative competitiveness of the proposal.

Some case studies weaken the 'real unlabeled data' narrative: in the Hodgkin-Huxley experiment the 'unlabeled' data are themselves simulated (θ ~ Normal(0,2)); only the air traffic and MNIST studies use genuinely real unlabeled data.

Evaluation in the image case study is largely qualitative (visual inspection of means, SD maps, and samples) without quantitative metrics (e.g., reconstruction error, calibration measures), making it difficult to assess the magnitude of improvement.

Empirical robustness even 'far beyond both training spaces' (e.g., µ_obs > 3 in the MVN study) is an intriguing but surprising extrapolation result that is observed only on a toy Gaussian problem and not explained theoretically; supporting evidence on more complex models is needed for this strong claim.

strengths: Clear and meaningful contribution: extends Bayesian self-consistency (SC) losses from fully supervised, simulation-only settings to semi-supervised training with unlabeled data, addressing a well-recognized weakness of amortized Bayesian inference (out-of-simulation robustness).

Solid theoretical grounding: Propositions 1-4 with complete proofs show that SC losses (and the combined semi-supervised loss) are strictly proper and agnostic to the unlabeled data distribution, so there is no accuracy-robustness trade-off — a clean and practically important property distinguishing the method from regularizer-based or UDA approaches.

Comprehensive evaluation across four diverse case studies: a controllable multivariate normal problem with analytic posteriors and thorough factor ablations (dimensionality, number/mean of unlabeled observations, summary network, estimated vs. known likelihood), a real-data autoregressive application benchmarked against Stan, the high-dimensional Hodgkin-Huxley model, and a 784-dimensional MNIST denoising task (NPLE).

Appropriate baselines and honest comparisons: standard NPE, NPE-MMD, NPE-DANN, NNPE, VAE, online NPE, and prior self-consistency work (Schmitt et al., 2024) are compared; error bars over 10 refits; metrics include MMD, posterior mean/SD bias, and Wasserstein distance.

Impressive data efficiency (robustness gains with as few as 4 unlabeled observations) and amortization is fully preserved, plus a thoughtful discussion of limitations (variance-based loss requires fast density evaluation, unsuitable for flow matching/diffusion), a reproducibility statement, detailed appendix setups, and code availability.
weaknesses: Applicability hinge: the SC loss requires evaluating a (known or neural) likelihood density on the unlabeled data. For genuinely misspecified models, evaluating p(x*|θ) on out-of-support real data can be numerically uninformative (near-zero likelihoods), and the paper acknowledges that the estimated-likelihood case does not yet match the known-likelihood case — this limits real-world deployment where likelihoods are the hardest to specify.

Conceptual scope of 'robustness': the method targets the analytic posterior of the *specified* model. Under true model misspecification, this posterior is itself not the posterior under the real data-generating process; the paper is careful about this but the headline framing ('robust ABI on real data') could still be over-interpreted by practitioners.

The unlabeled data in several experiments is simulated rather than real (e.g., Hodgkin-Huxley 'unlabeled' set from θ ~ Normal(0,2)), so the claim of using 'any real data' is only directly validated in the air-traffic and MNIST studies; a dedicated experiment with genuinely real unlabeled data under hard misspecification would strengthen the claims.

Theoretical results, while correct, are relatively straightforward (a consequence of C being minimized iff its argument is constant, plus additivity of proper losses); strict properness for the practical log-variance estimator with finite L samples and the chosen proposal q_t is asserted rather than analyzed in depth.

Minor presentation issues: duplicated paragraph in Appendix B (the Köthe (2023) motivation appears twice nearly verbatim), code URL appears incomplete in the abstract, and the strict-properness argument relies on an assumed class of scores C whose assumption is essentially tailored to the conclusion.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: extending Bayesian self-consistency (SC) losses to unlabeled, out-of-simulation data enables semi-supervised ABI without ground-truth parameters, which is a genuinely useful capability for the simulation-based inference community.

The theoretical contribution, while concise, is sound: the strict-properness results (Propositions 1–4) are correct, and the observation that the semi-supervised loss targets the analytic posterior without introducing a robustness/accuracy trade-off is a meaningful conceptual point that cleanly differentiates the method from regularization-based and generalized-Bayes alternatives.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad and multi-faceted: a controllable toy problem with analytic ground truth (including ablations over dimensionality, unlabeled dataset size, summary networks, and known vs. estimated likelihood), a real-data autoregressive case study validated against Stan (MCMC), a high-dimensional Hodgkin-Huxley model, and a challenging 784-dimensional NPLE image-denoising task.

Baselines are appropriate and fairly run: standard NPE, online NPE, Schmitt et al. (2024), VAE, NNPE, NPE-DANN, and NPE-MMD, with results showing the proposed method substantially outperforms competing robustness approaches under prior misspecification.
Reproducibility is good: architectures, hyperparameters, training schedules, and hardware are documented in detail in the appendices, with code promised and error bars over multiple model refits.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The self-consistency variance loss is taken directly from Schmitt et al. (2024), and the main extension (applying it to unlabeled observations instead of simulated ones) is a relatively small algorithmic change; the strict-properness proofs are short corollaries of existing results (Köthe, 2023) and the identity in Eq. (1) is elementary. The contribution may be seen as more of a careful empirical demonstration than a fundamental advance.

The 'real unlabeled data' narrative is overstated in places. In the multivariate normal study, the unlabeled data x* are simulated from Normal(µ*, I), and in the Hodgkin-Huxley study the pool of M=1,024 unlabeled observations is likewise simulated from θ ~ Normal(0, 2) rather than obtained from real measurements. Only the air-traffic and MNIST case studies use genuinely empirical unlabeled data, so the headline claim that robustness holds on 'real data originating from any source' rests on fewer experiments than the abstract suggests.

The method's target under misspecification deserves more critical discussion. When p*(x) ≠ p(x), the SC loss pulls the estimator toward the analytic posterior of the (misspecified) model, not the posterior under the true data-generating process; whether this is the desired behavior in scientific applications is debatable and is only briefly addressed in Appendix B.

Practical applicability is limited by the requirement that q(θ | x) admit fast, exact density evaluation; the authors themselves note that flow matching and diffusion-based posterior estimators are incompatible with the current loss, which excludes much of the modern generative-modeling toolbox. Whether the SC signal extends to estimated likelihoods is only partially resolved (residual posterior SD bias remains in Figure 7).

Some presentation issues: the code link in the abstract is incomplete ('The code is available at' with no URL), Appendix B contains a duplicated paragraph (the Köthe motivation appears twice verbatim), and Figure 1 labels reference a gray triangle that is difficult to see against the gray reference contours.

Significance is strongest for the SBI/amortized-inference sub-community; impact on the broader AI audience is moderate, and the experiments, while diverse, are all in settings where the analytic or MCMC-computable model posterior is available, leaving open how the method behaves on truly complex simulators where no gold standard exists.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and addresses a genuine, widely recognized weakness of amortized Bayesian inference: posterior bias under simulation gaps and model misspecification.

The semi-supervised formulation is elegant: the self-consistency loss provably targets the analytic posterior regardless of the unlabeled data distribution (Proposition 3), so there is no accuracy-robustness trade-off in the training objective - a clean contrast with regularization-based alternatives.

Good theoretical grounding: the strict-properness propositions (including the variant for likelihood estimators) are stated precisely with proofs, and the distinction between the known-likelihood and joint-estimation settings is honestly discussed.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four case studies spanning a controllable toy problem (with ablations over dimensionality, unlabeled data size, likelihood type, and summary networks), a real-data time-series application benchmarked against Stan, a high-dimensional ODE model, and a 784-dimensional image denoising task.
Honest limitations section (incompatibility with free-form flows, degraded results with estimated likelihoods), reproducibility statement, and computational resource reporting.
Baselines include reasonable competitors (NPE-DANN, NPE-MMD, NNPE, VAE, Schmitt et al. 2024), and the appendix comparisons are informative.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is modest: Propositions 1-4 are short corollaries of Bayes' rule and the known variance-based SC loss of Schmitt et al. (2024); the main novelty is extending these to unlabeled data, and the proofs are elementary. Strict properness concerns only global minima and says nothing about optimization dynamics, which is where the empirical gains actually originate.

The method requires a density-evaluable posterior and an (analytic or separately learned) likelihood. The guarantees evaporate in the NPLE setting, and the paper's own results (Figure 7) show noticeably larger posterior SD bias and MMD with an estimated likelihood - precisely the regime where 'any source' unlabeled data would be most needed. The practical scope is thus narrower than the abstract suggests.

Baseline coverage is uneven: comparisons to NPE-DANN, NPE-MMD, and NNPE appear only for the 2D toy problem, while the flagship real-world case studies (air traffic, Hodgkin-Huxley, MNIST) are compared mainly against plain NPE and Stan. Broader comparisons on the realistic tasks would strengthen the central claims.

The mechanism by which the SC loss enables extrapolation far outside the training distribution (e.g., mu_obs > 3) remains largely unexplained; the result appears sensitive to training dynamics, and the reported non-monotonic behavior across M in Table 1 (M=4 sometimes better than M=8) hints at instability that is not analyzed.
Presentation issues: the code link in the abstract is empty; the paragraph on the variance-loss motivation is duplicated verbatim in Appendix B; Figure 1's axis labels are truncated.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'drastically improves robustness' and 'generalizing beyond both labeled and unlabeled training data' rest primarily on the Gaussian case study with a conjugate analytic posterior; robustness claims under more realistic misspecification are less thoroughly quantified.
